newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian labour force data - review of forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Australian labour force data - review of forecasts.

text.p: Australian employment data for June will be released today at 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT).
Forecasts for June employment centre on a rise of 42,500. This would reverse the 40,300 fall in May, and forecasts range from a rise of 25,000 to a rise of 60,000.
Unemployment rate forecasts centre on 8.7 percent, down a notch from May's 8.8 percent. Forecasts range from 8.6 to 8.9 percent.
Recent data, and June forecasts, are detailed below.
Employment Jan Feb March April May June(f)
The June rise is seen as a statistical correction to the May fall, and economists said that given the weakness seen so far in 1997, the risks to forecasts were to the topside.
However, it would take a rise near 100,000 jobs to seriously challenge the market's perception that the labour market is weak and justifying another rate cut.
The expected rise would mean employment levels were 1.1 percent higher than in June last year.
In the first five months of 1997, employment has actually fallen 15,900. A 42,500 rise in June would mean employment has risen by under 4,500 per month in the first half of 1997.
The weakest area has been full-time employment. Over the first five months of 1997, it has fallen by 47,000, while part-time employment has risen by 31,100.

If unemployment comes in as forecast, it will be the 11th time in the 1996/97 (July/June) fiscal year that unemployment has been at or above 8.6 percent. The lowest unemployment rate so far in 1996/97 has been 8.5 percent, registered in November.

The stalling of unemployment above 8.5 percent has been a key factor in the four rate cuts seen since July 31 last year. Continued high unemployment will buoy market expectations of a rate cut occurring in the next month, analysts said.

The unemployment rate would not get any help from an expected rise in the participation rate, unlike in May when analysts said a 0.3 percentage point fall in the participation rate was all that stopped it from edging over 9.0 percent.
Macquarie Bank economists said a 30,000 rise in employment would see unemployment at 8.6 percent on a 63.2 percent participation rate.
Should the participation rate rise to 63.4, the median market forecast, the unemployment rate would be 8.9 percent on a 30,000 rise and 8.7 percent on a 50,000 rise, Macquarie said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
